2027-05-29.title: Saturday of the Eighth Week in Ordinary Time · St Paul VI, Pope
readings: While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer
The precepts of the Lord give joy to the heart
By what authority are you doing these things?
2027-05-29.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 8 (Year I). St Paul VI, pope, may be remembered (optional memorial, inscribed in the General Roman Calendar in 2019). A Mass of the Blessed Virgin Mary on Saturday may also be celebrated. First reading and psalm in NRSV numbering. Liturgical colour: green (white if a memorial is kept).
2027-05-29.verse: More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey, and drippings of the honeycomb.
theo: The Book of Sirach ends with a short autobiography in the form of a poem. The old teacher looks back and tells his students how he found wisdom. It began with thanksgiving: he blesses the name of the Lord who rescued him in time of trouble. Then he remembers his youth: “While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer. Before the temple I asked for her, and I will search for her until the end.” Wisdom is not first a set of clever ideas; it is something asked for in prayer, before God's house. He uses the image of a vine: “From the first blossom to the ripening grape my heart delighted in her; my foot walked on the straight path; from my youth I followed her steps.” Growth was slow but steady: “I inclined my ear a little and received her, and I found for myself much instruction. I made progress in her; to him who gives wisdom I will give glory.” It also took effort: “My soul grappled with wisdom, and in my conduct I was strict.” And the fruit was purity of heart: “I directed my soul to her, and in purity I found her.” The Psalm praises God's law in the same spirit: “the precepts of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart; the commandment of the LORD is clear, enlightening the eyes,” “sweeter also than honey, and drippings of the honeycomb.” As schools in Kerala and across India prepare to reopen, these lines are a prayer for every student: seek wisdom on your knees, and keep seeking her to the end.

In the Gospel Jesus is walking in the Temple the day after he drove out the traders, and the chief priests, the scribes and the elders come with a sharp question: “By what authority are you doing these things? Who gave you this authority to do them?” It is a fair question for the guardians of the Temple to ask. Jesus answers with a question of his own: “Did the baptism of John come from heaven, or was it of human origin? Answer me.” The leaders discuss it among themselves. If they say from heaven, he will ask why they did not believe John; if they say of human origin, they fear the crowd, “for all regarded John as truly a prophet.” So they answer, “We do not know.” And Jesus says, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things.” Jesus is not playing a clever game. John had pointed to Jesus; anyone who accepted John's witness would already know where Jesus' authority came from. But the question cannot be answered by calculation, by asking what is safe to say. It needs a heart that seeks the truth, as Ben Sira sought wisdom. This is not a judgment on a whole people; these were particular men in a particular moment, and the same temptation to measure the truth by what others will think lives in every one of us. Today the Church may remember St Paul VI, the pope who guided the Second Vatican Council to its end. He knew the weight of authority, and he used it as a servant: in 1964 he laid the papal tiara on the altar of St Peter's as a gift for the poor, and in the same year he came to Bombay for the International Eucharistic Congress, the first pope ever to visit India. He wrote that people today listen more willingly to witnesses than to teachers (Evangelii Nuntiandi 41, in substance). Authority in the Church is credible when it is a witness to the truth.
outline: Ask: when you have to decide what is true, do you ask “What is right?” or “What will people think?”
Point 1 · Sought in prayer from youth
Ben Sira found wisdom by asking for it before God's house and following her steps.
God's law rejoices the heart and enlightens the eyes.
An answer that needs a heart open to the truth, not a calculation.
“I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.”
live: Before you begin your work or study today, pray: Lord, give me wisdom for this task.
Today, when it would be easier to say “I do not know” to avoid trouble, speak the truth kindly and simply.
2027-05-29.prayer: Lord God, giver of wisdom, from our youth teach us to seek you in prayer and to follow wisdom's steps until the end. Make your precepts sweeter to us than honey, and let your commandment enlighten our eyes. Lord Jesus, your authority comes from the Father; give us hearts that seek the truth and do not measure it by the fear of others. Through the prayers of St Paul VI, may all who hold authority in the Church be humble servants and faithful witnesses. Amen.
altar: Ben Sira asked for wisdom “before the temple.” We come before the altar where Wisdom himself, the eternal Word made flesh, gives us his Body and Blood. Here the question “By what authority?” is answered: by the authority of the Son who loved us to the end and offers himself to the Father for us.

quick: At the end of his book Ben Sira tells how he sought wisdom in prayer from his youth and found her in purity of heart.
God's law is sweeter than honey and enlightens the eyes.
Asked by what authority he acts, Jesus asks about John's baptism; the leaders, afraid of the crowd, say: We do not know.
2027-05-29.action: Before any study or work today, pray: Lord, give me wisdom.
2027-05-29.question: Do I decide what is true by asking what is right, or by asking what others will think?
kidsaint: Paul VI was the Pope about fifty years ago. He was the first Pope to travel by aeroplane to many countries, and in 1964 he came to India, to Bombay, for a big celebration of Jesus in the Eucharist. Huge crowds came to see him. He loved the poor so much that he gave away the Pope's beautiful crown, the tiara, to help them, and he gave the car he used in Bombay to Mother Teresa for her work. Lesson: the more important you are, the more you should serve others.

family.explain: A wise man in the Bible tells us: when I was young I prayed to God and asked him for wisdom. Wisdom means knowing what is good and right and doing it. The psalm says that God's words are sweeter than honey! Soon school will start again. Let us ask God to make us wise, not only clever.
family.intention: We pray for children and students preparing for the new school year, and for their teachers.
family.ask: Ask: “What is the difference between being clever and being wise?”

illus: When St Paul VI landed in Bombay in December 1964 for the International Eucharistic Congress, he was the first pope ever to set foot in India. Huge crowds of Christians, Hindus, Muslims and others lined the roads. In one of his talks he spoke of the people of India as seekers of God, and he prayed for peace and for the hungry. Before leaving he gave the white car he had used during the visit to Mother Teresa; she raffled it and used the money for her work among people with leprosy. The pope's authority became a gift for the poorest.

pm.open: Lord, giver of wisdom, open our hearts to your truth and make your word sweeter to us than honey. Amen.
share: While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer (Sirach 51:13). Do I ask God for wisdom before my decisions?
The precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart (Psalm 19:8). Which commandment of God has brought me joy rather than burden?
We do not know (Mark 11:33). When have I avoided the truth because I feared what others would think?
pm.resp: The precepts of the Lord give joy to the heart.
interc: For the Pope and the bishops, that their authority may always be a service and a witness, through the prayers of St Paul VI.
For students and teachers as the new academic year begins.
For young people seeking their path in life, that they may seek wisdom in prayer.
For all who are afraid to speak the truth, that they may receive courage.
For our group, that God's word may be sweeter to us than honey.
pm.close: Father, you give wisdom to those who ask. Make us humble seekers of your truth and faithful witnesses of your Son. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, at the end of his long book Ben Sira tells us his own story. While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer. Before the temple I asked for her, and I will search for her until the end (Sirach 51:13–14). He did not find wisdom first in books. He found her on his knees.

He also says that wisdom grew in him slowly, like grapes on a vine, from the first blossom to the ripening grape. And it took effort: my soul grappled with wisdom. And it needed a clean heart: in purity I found her (Sirach 51:20). Many children will soon go back to school. Let us pray that they become not only clever but wise, and that they learn, like Ben Sira, to ask God for wisdom.

In the Gospel the leaders ask Jesus: by what authority are you doing these things? Jesus asks them about John the Baptist: was his baptism from heaven or of human origin? They do not ask what is true. They ask what is safe. If we say this, he will say that; if we say that, the crowd will be angry. So they answer: we do not know (Mark 11:33). The same temptation lives in us: to decide what is true by what others will think.

Jesus' authority comes from his Father, and we receive it with an open heart. St Paul VI, whom we may remember today, held great authority as pope. But he laid down the papal crown for the poor and came to India to honour Jesus in the Eucharist. He taught that people listen to witnesses more than to teachers. Let us ask today for wisdom, for an honest heart, and for the courage to be witnesses of the truth. Amen.
kids: Children, a wise man in the Bible says: when I was young, I prayed and asked God to make me wise. Being wise means knowing what is good and choosing it. The psalm says God's words are sweeter than honey! Soon school will begin. Every morning, before you study, say a little prayer: Jesus, help me to learn, and make me wise and good.

intro: Theme: “I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.”
Wisdom sought from youth, a law sweeter than honey, and a question that only an honest heart can answer.

q: While I was still young, before I went on my travels, I sought wisdom openly in my prayer.
If any of you is lacking in wisdom, ask God, who gives to all generously and ungrudgingly, and it will be given you.
points.apply: Each morning this week, before work or study, ask God for wisdom in one sentence of prayer.

sub: The law that revives the soul.
q: More to be desired are they than gold, even much fine gold; sweeter also than honey, and drippings of the honeycomb.
for he taught them as one having authority, and not as their scribes.
points.apply: Read one chapter of a Gospel slowly this week, and stop at the verse that tastes sweetest to you.

q: The fear of others lays a snare, but one who trusts in the Lord is secure.
For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to testify to the truth. Everyone who belongs to the truth listens to my voice.
points.apply: This week, in one situation where you are tempted to hide the truth for fear of others, speak it gently and clearly.

concl: Ben Sira found wisdom by seeking her in prayer from his youth until his old age.
Jesus' authority is recognised not by calculation but by hearts that seek the truth; St Paul VI showed that authority is credible when it serves and witnesses.
2027-05-29.resolve: Begin every task this week with a short prayer for wisdom.
